name_native: น้ำดอกอัญชัน (nam dok anchan)
cultivar: Clitoria ternatea, a climbing legume with deep-blue flowers
processing: Flowers are picked in the morning, laid out and sun- or oven-dried whole; a smaller amount is milled into a fine blue powder.
harvest_season: The vine flowers almost year-round in the tropics, so there is no fixed season; picking is continuous, with more flowers in the rainy season.
appearance_dry: Whole papery flowers of a deep violet-blue with a paler yellowish keel, light as tissue.
appearance_liquor: Vivid cobalt blue, clear; a squeeze of lemon or lime turns it violet to magenta.
appearance_wet: Limp blue-purple flowers that have given up most of their colour.
taste_profile: Very mild: a faint green, pea-like, slightly woody taste with little aroma; the point is the colour rather than the flavour.

brewing.notes: 5–8 flowers per cup, just-boiled water, 4–5 minutes; more flowers give a deeper blue but no more taste. Add citrus at the table for the colour change. In Thailand it is usually sweetened with sugar or honey and served over ice with lime.

vintage_note: Sold year-round with no harvest date, as whole dried flowers (loose or in bags) or as powder marketed as 'blue matcha', which is simply ground petals and has nothing to do with tea. The blue pigment fades with light and age, so a pack should be stored in the dark and used within a year of opening; a best-before of one to two years is typical. Flowers that look grey-violet rather than deep blue are old and brew pale.
description:
Butterfly pea flower is the one that turns the cup blue. The dried flowers of a tropical vine give an infusion the colour of ink, and because the pigment is a natural pH indicator, a squeeze of lime shifts it to purple and then pink in front of your eyes. In Thailand it has long been a sweet iced drink and a natural food colouring for rice and desserts; in the West it arrived only in recent years, mostly through travel shows, food blogs and cocktails.

Processing is nothing more than picking and drying the whole flowers, so the quality is about colour: fresh stock is a deep, saturated blue and gives a strong cup from a handful of flowers, while old stock has faded to grey-violet and brews weak.

What surprises people is how little it tastes of anything. There is a mild green, pea-pod note and a faint woodiness, no bitterness and no real aroma, so it is almost always sweetened, iced or blended. Four to five minutes with hot water is plenty; longer only deepens the colour. Lemongrass, ginger, mint and citrus all work with it, and a plain blue brew over ice with lime and honey is the standard Thai serve.

It is sold as whole flowers or as a powder sometimes called blue matcha; the powder is just milled petals and should be priced like a food colouring, not like Japanese tea. Store it away from light.

Treat it as a colour and a base, not a flavour: it makes blue lemonade, layered iced teas and a purple cold brew with hibiscus, and it is a fun one to show children.
history:
Clitoria ternatea is common across Southeast Asia, and its flowers have long been used there both for herbal drinks and as a blue dye for food, as in the rice dish nasi kerabu. In Thailand and Vietnam the infusion is mixed with honey and lemon and served after dinner or as a refreshment in hotels and spas; the Thai name is nam dok anchan. No early date for the drink itself is well documented, and the usual claim is simply that it goes back centuries.

The wider world found it only recently, through travel shows, food blogs and bartenders who liked the colour change: acid turns the blue to purple, and hibiscus takes it to bright red. In 2021 the US Food and Drug Administration declared butterfly pea flower extract exempt from certification and safe for use as an additive.
